claim: MCTP was identified in a forward genetic screen for mutations that block presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP).
source: In a forward genetic screen for mutations that block PHP we identified mctp (Multiple C2 Domain Proteins with Two Transmembrane Regions).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that mctp was identified in a forward genetic screen for PHP mutations.

claim: MCTP localizes to the membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) throughout the soma, dendrites, axon and presynaptic terminal.
source: Here we show that MCTP localizes to the membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) that elaborate throughout the soma, dendrites, axon and presynaptic terminal.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states MCTP localization, and this is supported by imaging data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: MCTP functions downstream of presynaptic calcium influx.
source: Then, we demonstrate that MCTP functions downstream of presynaptic calcium influx with separable activities to stabilize baseline transmission, short-term release dynamics and PHP.
evidence: The abstract states this conclusion, which is supported by calcium imaging experiments showing no change in presynaptic calcium influx in mctp mutants (Figure 6).

claim: PHP specifically requires the calcium coordinating residues in each of the three C2 domains of MCTP.
source: Notably, PHP specifically requires the calcium coordinating residues in each of the three C2 domains of MCTP.
evidence: The abstract states this, supported by experiments showing that mutations in individual C2 domains block PHP (Figure 10).

claim: MCTP is proposed as a novel, ER-localized calcium sensor for homeostatic stabilization of neurotransmission.
source: Thus, we propose MCTP as a novel, ER-localized calcium sensor and a source of calcium-dependent feedback for the homeostatic stabilization of neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the combined evidence of ER localization, calcium-binding requirements, and functional role in PHP.

claim: Presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP) is conserved from Drosophila to human.
source: The homeostatic modulation of presynaptic neurotransmitter release, termed presynaptic homeostatic plasticity (PHP), is highly conserved from Drosophila to human (Davis, 2013; Davis and Müller, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: PHP can be rapidly induced on a time scale of seconds to minutes.
source: PHP can be rapidly induced on a time scale of seconds to minutes, can precisely adjust the presynaptic release mechanism to offset a wide range of postsynaptic perturbations and can be stably maintained for the life of an organism; months in Drosophila (Mahoney et al., 2014) and decades in human (Cull-Candy et al., 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: PHP can be stably maintained for months in Drosophila and decades in humans.
source: PHP can be rapidly induced on a time scale of seconds to minutes, can precisely adjust the presynaptic release mechanism to offset a wide range of postsynaptic perturbations and can be stably maintained for the life of an organism; months in Drosophila (Mahoney et al., 2014) and decades in human (Cull-Candy et al., 1980).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: MCTPs are evolutionarily conserved proteins with three C2 domains and two C-terminal membrane-spanning domains.
source: MCTPs are evolutionarily conserved proteins with three C2 domains and two C-terminal membrane-spanning domains (Shin et al., 2005).
evidence: This structural description is supported by a citation.

claim: The C2 domains of MCTP can bind calcium with relatively high affinity (1–2.5 µM) in the apparent absence of phospholipid binding.
source: The C2 domains are unusual in that they are able to bind calcium with relatively high affinity (1–2.5 µM) and do so in the apparent absence of phospholipid binding (Shin et al., 2005).
evidence: This biochemical property is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Genetic deletion of mctp in C. elegans is embryonic lethal.
source: In C. elegans, genetic deletion of mctp is embryonic lethal (Maeda et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Genetic mutations in mctp have been linked to bipolar disorder in mammals.
source: In mammals, mctp is expressed in the brain and spinal cord and genetic mutations in mctp have been linked to bipolar disorder (Djurovic et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009).
evidence: This association is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: PHP is completely blocked in all three mctp mutants (mctp1, mctp2, and mctpOG9).
source: First, we demonstrate that PHP is completely blocked in all three mctp mutants, as well as when mctp1 is placed in trans to the mctp deficiency (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1.

claim: Application of PhTx causes a significant decrease in mEPSP amplitude in wild type and all mctp mutant combinations.
source: More specifically, application of sub-blocking concentrations of PhTx causes a significant decrease in mEPSP amplitude in wild type and in all of the mctp mutant combinations that we tested (Figure 1D; Student's t-test; p<0.01 for each genotype, comparing the absence versus presence of PhTx).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: In wild type, there is a homeostatic increase in quantal content that precisely offsets the decrease in mEPSP amplitude and restores EPSP amplitudes to baseline.
source: In wild type, there is a homeostatic increase in quantal content (EPSP/mEPSP; Figure 1F; p<0.01) that precisely offsets the decrease in mEPSP amplitude and restores EPSP amplitudes to baseline (Figure 1B,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 1B, E, and F.

claim: In all four mctp mutant combinations, the homeostatic increase in quantal content is blocked.
source: However, in all four mctp mutant combinations, the homeostatic increase in quantal content is blocked (Figure 1F; p>0.05 for each genotype relative to baseline in the absence of PhTx) and EPSP amplitudes remain smaller than baseline (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 1E and F with statistical analysis.

claim: All mctp mutant alleles have diminished average EPSP amplitudes compared to wild type at baseline.
source: However, all mutant alleles have diminished average EPSP amplitudes compared to wild type (Figure 1E, solid bars; p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 1E with statistical analysis.

claim: Calculated quantal content is significantly decreased in mctp1, mctp2 and mctpOG9 at baseline.
source: Calculated quantal content is significantly decreased in mctp1, mctp2 and mctpOG9 (Figure 1F, solid bars; p<0.05).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: Neuron-specific expression of UAS-mctp in the mctp1 mutant background fully rescues PHP.
source: Neuron-specific expression of UAS-mctp in the mctp1 mutant background ('rescue neuron' in Figure 1G–J) fully rescues PHP as demonstrated by a large increase in quantal content and the restoration of EPSP amplitudes to baseline values in the presence of PhTx (Figure 1G–J; p>0.5 compared to wild type for mEPSP, EPSP and quantal content values).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 1G-J with statistical analysis.

claim: Muscle-specific expression of UAS-mctp does not rescue PHP.
source: By contrast, muscle-specific expression of UAS-mctp ('rescue muscle' in Figure 1G–J) does not rescue PHP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 1G-J.

claim: MCTP activity is necessary in the presynaptic neuron for PHP.
source: Regardless, taken together, these data confirm that mctp is essential for the rapid induction of PHP and that MCTP activity is necessary in the presynaptic neuron for PHP.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the rescue experiments showing neuronal but not muscle rescue of PHP.

claim: The GluRIIA mutant has decreased mEPSP amplitudes and a robust, homeostatic increase in quantal content.
source: Here, we confirm that the GluRIIA mutant has decreased mEPSP amplitudes and a robust, homeostatic increase in quantal content (p<0.01).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 2 with statistical analysis.

claim: PHP is completely blocked in the mctp1,GluRIIA double mutant.
source: However, when PHP is assessed in the mctp1,GluRIIA double mutant, PHP is completely blocked (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 2.

claim: In mctp1,GluRIIA double mutants, mEPSP amplitudes are decreased to levels identical to that observed in the GluRIIA mutant.
source: More specifically, in mctp1,GluRIIA double mutants, mEPSP amplitudes are decreased to levels identical to that observed in the GluRIIA mutant (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 2.

claim: In mctp1,GluRIIA double mutants, there is a failure to increase quantal content.
source: But, unlike the GluRIIA mutant, there is a failure to increase quantal content (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 2.

claim: Presynaptic expression of UAS-mctp fully restores PHP in the mctp1,GluRIIA double mutant background.
source: The specificity of this effect is confirmed by genetic rescue experiments. Presynaptic expression of UAS-mctp fully restores PHP in the mctp1,GluRIIA double mutant background (Figure 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 2.

claim: MCTP-Flag localizes to a reticulated, peri-nuclear membrane system within the soma.
source: Within the soma, MCTP concentrates within a reticulated, peri-nuclear membrane system (Figure 3A) and co-localizes with co-expressed ER-resident KDEL-RFP (not shown), indicative of ER localization.
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: MCTP-Flag extends into the axon on reticulated internal membranes.
source: MCTP-Flag is observed to extend into the axon on similarly reticulated internal membranes (Figure 3A and inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3A.

claim: MCTP-Flag extends throughout the dendrites and to the presynaptic nerve terminal.
source: MCTP-Flag extends throughout the dendrites (Figure 3A) and then extends all the way to the presynaptic nerve terminal (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: MCTP-Flag co-localizes with the ER resident protein HDEL-GFP in presynaptic terminals.
source: Consistent with this prior work, we demonstrate co-localization of MCTP-Flag with the ER resident protein HDEL-GFP (Summerville et al., 2016) in presynaptic terminals (Figure 3B, see also inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 3B showing co-localization.

claim: The isolated transmembrane domains of MCTP are sufficient to localize GFP to the ER in S2 cells.
source: We demonstrate that the isolated transmembrane domains of MCTP are sufficient to localize GFP to the ER, defined by co-localization with ER-tracker (Figure 3E, compare full length MCTP-GFP to TM only GFP).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in S2 cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: When the two transmembrane domains of MCTP are removed from MCTP-GFP, the truncated protein no longer localizes to the ER.
source: When the two transmembrane domains of MCTP are removed from MCTP-GFP, the truncated protein no longer localizes to the ER and is found broadly distributed (Figure 3E, MCTP noTM GFP).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in S2 cells shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Full length MCTP-GFP protein was never observed to reside on the cell plasma membrane.
source: Finally, we note that full length MCTP-GFP protein was never observed to reside on the cell plasma membrane (Figure 3E and data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on imaging observations in Figure 3E and additional unpublished data.

claim: MCTP-Flag does not co-localize with anti-Brp, but does come into close proximity at many active zones.
source: Single sections reveal that MCTP-Flag does not co-localize with anti-Brp, but does come into close proximity at many, though not all, active zones (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by super-resolution imaging data in Figure 3C.

claim: MCTP is essentially absent from clusters of synaptic vesicles identified by anti-Syt1 staining.
source: We note that MCTP is essentially absent from clusters of synaptic vesicles, identified by anti-Syt1 staining (Figure 4B arrows).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4B.

claim: There is a small but statistically significant increase in bouton number in both the mctp1 and mctp2 mutants compared to wild type.
source: We find a small, but statistically significant, increase in bouton number in both mctp1 and mctp2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of NMJ morphology in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is no significant change in active zone number or active zone density in mctp mutants.
source: We also quantified active zone number, assessed by counting the number of anti-Brp puncta that identify the presynaptic T-bar, resident at individual active zones. There is also no significant change in active zone number or active zone density (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mctp mutant NMJ appears morphologically normal, without satellite boutons or evidence of NMJ degeneration.
source: Beyond this, the mctp mutant NMJ appears morphologically normal, without the appearance of satellite boutons (Marie et al., 2004) and without any evidence of NMJ degeneration (Eaton et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated based on morphological observations with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Anti-Futsch staining is qualitatively normal in mctp mutants, consistent with normal NMJ growth and integrity.
source: We find that anti-Futsch staining is qualitatively normal, consistent with normal NMJ growth and normal NMJ integrity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EPSC amplitudes are significantly impaired in mctpOG9 across a 5-fold range of extracellular calcium (0.3–1.5 mM).
source: We repeated our analyses of baseline transmission using two-electrode voltage clamp to measure EPSC amplitudes across a 5-fold range of extracellular calcium (0.3–1.5 mM [Ca2+]e) and find that EPSC amplitudes are significantly impaired across this entire range (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 5A.

claim: There is an impaired calcium sensitivity of release in the mctpOG9 mutant without a change in the apparent calcium-cooperativity of release.
source: Thus, in the mctpOG9 mutant, there is an impaired calcium sensitivity of release (Figure 5A). This occurs without a change in the apparent calcium-cooperativity of release (see below), given that the magnitude of change is similar at all external calcium concentrations tested (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 5A showing parallel shifts across calcium concentrations.

claim: There is a significant change in short-term release dynamics in mctp mutants at 0.7, 1.0 and 1.5 mM [Ca2+]e.
source: Consistent with the conclusion mctp alters baseline release, we also find a significant change in short-term release dynamics at 0.7, 1.0 and 1.5 mM [Ca2+]e (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 5B.

claim: At 1.0 mM [Ca2+]e synaptic depression is observed at the wild type synapse compared to short-term facilitation at the mctp mutant synapse.
source: Indeed, at 1.0 mM [Ca2+]e synaptic depression is observed at the wild type synapse compared to short-term facilitation at the mctp mutant synapse (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 5B.

claim: The readily releasable vesicle pool (RRP) is unchanged in mctpOG9.
source: First, we demonstrate that the RRP is unchanged in mctpOG9 (Figure 5C–F), estimated following repetitive nerve stimulation at elevated extracellular calcium according to standard methods (Schneggenburger et al., 1999; Müller et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 5C-F using established methods.

claim: The estimated RRP for wild type is 953 (±56) compared to 1075 (±67) for mctp, which is not significantly different.
source: The estimated RRP for wild type is 953 (±56) compared to 1075 (±67) for mctp (n.s.; p>0.05, t-test, two tailed).
evidence: This is stated with specific quantitative values and statistical analysis.

claim: There is no change in EPSC rise time in mctp mutants.
source: We also demonstrate that there is no change in EPSC rise time (Figure 5C) nor is there a change in the cumulative EPSC comparing wild type and the mctp mutant (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 5C and 5E.

claim: There is a significant 21% decrease in Ptrain for mctp compared to wild type.
source: Quantitatively, we find a significant 21% decrease in Ptrain for mctp compared to wild type (p<0.01, t-test, two-tailed, N = 10),
evidence: This is stated with specific quantitative values and statistical analysis.

claim: There is no difference in the action potential induced, spatially averaged calcium signal comparing wild type and the mctpOG9 mutant.
source: Surprisingly, we find no difference in the action potential induced, spatially averaged calcium signal comparing wild type and the mctpOG9 mutant (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figures 6A and 6B.

claim: There was no change in the time constant of OGB-1 signal decay in mctp mutants, consistent with no significant impact on presynaptic calcium buffering.
source: There was no change in the time constant of OGB-1 signal decay, consistent with the conclusion that the loss of MCTP does not significantly impact presynaptic calcium buffering (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data in Figure 6C.

claim: MCTP must act downstream of presynaptic calcium influx to influence synaptic vesicle release and short-term release dynamics.
source: These data demonstrate that MCTP must act downstream of presynaptic calcium influx in order to influence synaptic vesicle release and short-term release dynamics.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that calcium influx is normal but release is impaired in mctp mutants.

claim: At the wild type synapse, the presence of EGTA-AM causes a significant decrease in EPSC amplitude.
source: At the wild type synapse, the presence of EGTA-AM causes a significant decrease in EPSC amplitude.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: EPSCs in mctpOG9 mutants are completely insensitive to EGTA-AM.
source: In contrast, EPSCs in mctpOG9 mutants are completely insensitive to EGTA-AM (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 7B.

claim: EGTA-AM diminishes wild type EPSC amplitudes to precisely the levels observed in the mctp mutant in the absence of EGTA-AM.
source: We note that EGTA-AM diminishes wild type EPSC amplitudes to precisely the levels observed in the mctp mutant in the absence of EGTA-AM.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison of electrophysiological data in Figure 7.

claim: MCTP acts downstream of calcium influx to facilitate the release of an EGTA-sensitive vesicle pool during single action potential stimulation.
source: Since mctp is insensitive to EGTA-AM, we conclude that MCTP acts downstream of calcium influx to facilitate the release of an EGTA-sensitive vesicle pool during single action potential stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the EGTA-AM experiments showing differential effects in wild type versus mctp mutants.

claim: In mctp mutants, short-term facilitation is converted to short-term depression in the presence of EGTA-AM.
source: Thus, EGTA should convert facilitation to depression in mctp mutants. This is precisely what we observe.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 7A,B.

claim: MCTP is necessary to promote the fusion of a sub-population of synaptic vesicles that are weakly coupled to sites of action potential induced presynaptic calcium entry.
source: Thus, we provide evidence that MCTP is necessary to promote the fusion of a sub-population of synaptic vesicles that are weakly coupled to sites of action potential induced presynaptic calcium entry.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the EGTA-AM experiments and short-term plasticity data.

claim: In the presence of 25 µM EGTA-AM, the induction of PHP occurs normally.
source: In the presence of 25 µM EGTA-AM, the induction of PHP occurs normally (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 7C.

claim: At 125 µM EGTA-AM, baseline release is significantly impaired, reducing quantal content by ~50%, but statistically significant PHP is still observed.
source: Next, we increased the concentration of EGTA five-fold (125 µm), keeping the incubation time for EGTA-AM constant. In this condition, baseline release is significantly impaired, reducing quantal content by ~50%. None-the-less, we observe statistically significant PHP, although it is suppressed relative to controls in the absence of EGTA-AM (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 7D.

claim: PHP does not require the MCTP-dependent, EGTA-sensitive vesicle pool.
source: Thus, PHP does not require the MCTP-dependent, EGTA-sensitive vesicle pool.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that PHP can occur in the presence of EGTA-AM.

claim: MCTP appears to have an additional activity that is necessary for PHP beyond its role in promoting EGTA-sensitive vesicle release.
source: MCTP appears to have an additional activity that is necessary for PHP.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PHP requires MCTP but not the EGTA-sensitive vesicle pool.

claim: In wild type animals, PHP is normally expressed at all extracellular calcium concentrations tested (0.3 mm to 1.5 mM [Ca2+]e).
source: Consistent with prior evidence, in wild type animals, PHP is normally expressed at all extracellular calcium concentrations tested (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 8.

claim: mctp mutants revealed calcium sensitive expression of PHP.
source: However, mctp mutants revealed calcium sensitive expression of PHP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 8 showing differential PHP expression at different calcium concentrations.

claim: At low extracellular calcium (0.3 mm and 0.5 mM [Ca2+]e), PHP is completely blocked in mctpOG9.
source: At low extracellular calcium (0.3 mm and 0.5 mM [Ca2+]e), PHP is completely blocked in mctpOG9 (Figure 8, see also Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 8.

claim: When [Ca2+]e is elevated into the physiological range (0.7 mM and 1.0 mM [Ca2+]e), PHP remains blocked in mctpOG9.
source: When [Ca2+]e is elevated into the physiological range (0.7 mM and 1.0 mM [Ca2+]e), PHP remains blocked (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 8C.

claim: Only when [Ca2+]e is increased into the higher end of the physiological range (1.5 mM [Ca2+]e) is PHP expressed in mctpOG9.
source: Only when [Ca2+]e is increased into the higher end of the physiological range (1.5 mM [Ca2+]e) is PHP expressed in mctpOG9.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 8.

claim: MCTP normally functions to ensure that PHP is robustly and accurately expressed under variable [Ca2+]e conditions.
source: We propose that MCTP normally functions to ensure that PHP is robustly and accurately expressed under variable [Ca2+]e conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the calcium-dependent PHP expression in mctp mutants.

claim: There is no change in active zone ultrastructure or vesicle distribution in mctp mutants.
source: We find no change in active zone ultrastructure or vesicle distribution in mctp (Figure 9).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 9.

claim: There is no change in vesicle diameter in mctp mutants, indicative of normal vesicle recycling.
source: There is no change in vesicle diameter, indicative of normal vesicle recycling at this synapse (Poskanzer et al., 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 9 with citation to relevant literature.

claim: There is no change in the average number of vesicles per active zone in mctp mutants.
source: There is no change in the average number of vesicles per active zone, nor is there a change in the average vesicle distance from the center of the presynaptic T-bar, the site where presynaptic CaV2.1 calcium channels reside (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figures 9D-F.

claim: There is no change in the absolute length of the active zone in mctp mutants.
source: Finally, there is no change in the absolute length of the active zone, defined as the electron dense pre- and postsynaptic membranes that flank either side of a T-bar (Harris et al., 2015) (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data in Figure 9C with citation to methods.

claim: All three C2 domains of MCTP bind calcium.
source: It was previously demonstrated that all three C2 domains of MCTP bind calcium (Shin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Each mctp transgene (mctpC2A*, mctpC2B* and mctpC2C*) is well expressed and is distributed throughout the presynaptic terminal.
source: First, we demonstrate that each mctp transgene (mctpC2A*, mctpC2B* and mctpC2C*) is well expressed and is distributed throughout the presynaptic terminal (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging data in Figure 10A.

claim: All three C2 domain mutant transgenes (mctpC2A*, mctpC2B*, mctpC2C*) fail to rescue PHP in the mctpOG9 mutant background.
source: With this information in hand, we tested PHP and find that all three transgenes fail to rescue PHP in the mctpOG9 mutant background (Figure 10B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figures 10B and 10C.

claim: There is no increase in quantal content in mctp mutants expressing either UAS-mctpC2A* or UAS-mctpC2C*.
source: There is no increase in quantal content in mctp mutants expressing either UAS-mctpC2A* or UAS-mctpC2C*.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological data in Figure 10.

claim: MCTP functions as an ER-resident calcium sensor that is necessary for PHP.
source: We conclude that MCTP functions as an ER-resident calcium sensor that is necessary for PHP.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined evidence of ER localization, calcium-binding requirements, and functional role in PHP.

claim: PHP requires calcium-coordinating residues in all three MCTP C2 domains.
source: Since PHP requires calcium-coordinating residues in all three MCTP C2 domains, we propose that MCTP functions as a presynaptic calcium sensor and a source of calcium-feedback signaling to ensure robust expression of PHP.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the C2 domain mutation experiments showing that each domain is required for PHP.

claim: The smooth ER extends throughout the soma, dendrite, axon and presynaptic terminal in Drosophila and mammalian systems.
source: This is entirely consistent with recent studies in Drosophila and mammalian systems showing that the smooth ER extends throughout the soma, dendrite, axon and presynaptic terminal (de Juan-Sanz et al., 2017; Summerville et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The physiological range for extracellular calcium at the Drosophila NMJ is considered to be 0.7–2.2 mM.
source: The physiological range for extracellular calcium at the Drosophila NMJ is considered to be 0.7–2.2 mM (Stewart et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Extracellular calcium concentrations can be substantially diminished below the physiological range (hypocalcaemia) during periods of normal neural activity or as a consequence of disease in the mammalian central nervous system.
source: In the mammalian central nervous system, there is considerable evidence that extracellular calcium concentrations can be substantially diminished, well below the physiological range (hypocalcaemia) during periods of normal neural activity or as a consequence of disease (Lu et al., 2010; Borst and Sakmann, 1999; Silver and Erecińska, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The eSyts and orthologous Tricalbins in yeast are calcium sensitive molecular tethers that control the extent of ER-plasma membrane contact.
source: For example, the eSyts (Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015; Saheki et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2013) and orthologous Tricalbins in yeast (Manford et al., 2012; Toulmay and Prinz, 2012) are calcium sensitive molecular tethers that control the extent of ER-plasma membrane contact.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: One action of the eSyts is to control plasma membrane lipid homeostasis through the action of their SMP domain.
source: One action of the eSyts is to control plasma membrane lipid homeostasis through the action of their SMP domain (Saheki et al., 2016; Schauder et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Oligomerization of the ER-resident protein STIM1 occurs in response to lowered levels of calcium within the ER, triggering its interaction with and activation of the plasma membrane calcium channel Orai1.
source: As another example, it has been established that oligomerization of the ER-resident protein STIM1 occurs in response to lowered levels of calcium within the ER, triggering its interaction with and activation of the plasma membrane calcium channel Orai1. This represents a calcium-dependent signaling system that sustains calcium levels in the ER lumen (Feske et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2005; Liou et al., 2005) and has been recently linked to the regulation of presynaptic release under conditions of ER calcium depletion (de Juan-Sanz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: ER-plasma membrane contact sites exist prior to calcium-dependent STIM1 recruitment.
source: It is worth noting that ER-plasma membrane contact sites exist prior to calcium-dependent STIM1 recruitment, an observation that has highlighted the importance of ER-plasma membrane contact sites as platforms for other signaling events (Giordano et al., 2013; Anderie et al., 2007; Stefan et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Proteins resident at ER-plasma membrane contacts are not always selectively localized to these sites.
source: It is also worth noting that proteins resident at ER-plasma membrane contacts are not always selectively localized to these sites (Giordano et al., 2013), an observation that is consistent with the observed distribution of MCTP throughout the ER in neurons.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and related to the observed MCTP distribution.

claim: The spastic paraplegias are genetic disorders that include degeneration of upper motoneurons.
source: For example, the spastic paraplegias are genetic disorders that include degeneration of upper motoneurons (Blackstone et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Among the more than 70 gene mutations responsible for spastic paraplegias are mutations in the gene encoding ER-resident proteins Atlastin1 and Reticulon2.
source: Among the more than 70 gene mutations responsible for this disease are mutations in the gene encoding ER-resident proteins Atlastin1 and Reticulon2.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context and citation to published literature.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of either Atlastin1 or Reticulon2 in Drosophila motoneurons causes ER fragmentation, decreased neurotransmitter release and altered synaptic morphology.
source: A recent study demonstrated that RNAi-mediated knockdown of either gene in Drosophila motoneurons causes ER fragmentation, decreased neurotransmitter release and altered synaptic morphology (Summerville et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Mutations in Drosophila spastin, spartin and spichthyin disrupt the integrity of the ER membrane system.
source: Other recent studies have examined mutations in Drosophila spastin, spartin and spichthyin, all of which disrupt the integrity of the ER membrane system (Nahm et al., 2013; Ozdowski et al., 2011; Sherwood et al., 2004; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Mutations in spastin, spartin and spichthyin disrupt synaptic morphology, alter the microtubule cytoskeleton and cause defects in synaptic transmission.
source: Each of these mutations also disrupts synaptic morphology, alters the microtubule cytoskeleton and cause defects in synaptic transmission.
evidence: This statement is supported by the context and citations to published studies.

claim: Mutations in human mctp were recently associated with psychiatric disease in humans.
source: Finally, we extend our work to the analysis of calcium-coordinating residues in the individual C2 domains of MCTP and demonstrate that the distribution of C2-domain mutations are largely normal, implying that PHP is blocked while the ER membrane system remains intact. In this respect, it is very intriguing that mutations in human mctp were recently associated with psychiatric disease in humans (Djurovic et al., 2009; Scott et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Bipolar disorder can be considered a disease of neuronal malfunction that could reasonably be related to the role of MCTP in the homeostatic stabilization of synaptic transmission.
source: Bipolar disorder can be considered a disease of neuronal malfunction that could reasonably be related to the role of MCTP in the homeostatic stabilization of synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a speculative statement connecting the findings to human disease.

claim: The mctp1 transposon insertion resides in the non-coding, 3' untranslated region of the mctp gene and is predicted to be a loss of function allele.
source: The mctp1 transposon insertion resides in the non-coding, 3' untranslated region of the mctp gene and is predicted to be a loss of function allele.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the mutant alleles.

claim: The mctp2 transposon insertion resides within a coding exon and is predicted to be a molecular null mutation.
source: We acquired a second transposon insertion (mctp2) that resides within a coding exon that is predicted to be a molecular null mutation as well as a deficiency chromosome that uncovers the mctp locus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the mutant alleles.

claim: The mctpOG9 mutation is a single nucleotide insertion that creates a frame shift and an early stop codon at amino acid 132, predicted to be a molecular null.
source: In addition, using CRISPR-mediated gene editing, we generated a single nucleotide insertion that creates a frame shift and an early stop codon at amino acid 132, an mctp mutation that is predicted to be a molecular null (mctpOG9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the mutant alleles.

claim: All three mctp mutations are viable to the adult stage.
source: All three mutations are viable to the adult stage, allowing recordings to be made from normally sized NMJ at the third instar larval stage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the mutant alleles.

claim: MCTP does not change ER organization in the mctp mutant.
source: Second, we did not observe changes in ER organization in the mctp mutant and the microtubule cytoskeleton is unaltered in mctp.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion comparing mctp to other ER-related mutations.

claim: The microtubule cytoskeleton is unaltered in mctp mutants.
source: Second, we did not observe changes in ER organization in the mctp mutant and the microtubule cytoskeleton is unaltered in mctp.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by anti-Futsch staining data.

claim: There is no substantive change in NMJ growth, organization or changes in synaptic ultrastructure caused by loss of mctp.
source: Third, there is no substantive change in NMJ growth, organization or changes in synaptic ultrastructure caused by loss of mctp.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion and supported by morphological and EM data.

claim: The distribution of C2-domain mutations are largely normal, implying that PHP is blocked while the ER membrane system remains intact.
source: Finally, we extend our work to the analysis of calcium-coordinating residues in the individual C2 domains of MCTP and demonstrate that the distribution of C2-domain mutations are largely normal, implying that PHP is blocked while the ER membrane system remains intact.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion based on the C2 domain mutation experiments.

claim: MCTP-dependent stabilization of PHP could be an essential mechanism to prevent the failure of synaptic transmission at neuromuscular and possibly central synapses under convergent conditions of hypocalcaemia and homeostatic stress.
source: As such, MCTP-dependent stabilization of PHP could be an essential mechanism to prevent the failure of synaptic transmission at neuromuscular and, possibly, central synapses under convergent conditions of hypocalcaemia and homeostatic stress.
evidence: This is a speculative statement in the Discussion about the potential physiological role of MCTP.

claim: MCTP lacks an SMP domain.
source: MCTP lacks an SMP domain, but this does not rule out the possibility that MCTP functions as part of a related protein complex that mediates such an activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion comparing MCTP to eSyts.

claim: Depletion of ER calcium strongly suppresses presynaptic release in a STIM1-dependent manner.
source: In this work, depletion of ER calcium strongly suppresses presynaptic release in a STIM1-dependent manner (de Juan-Sanz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: STIM-1 knockdown was shown to have no effect on baseline transmission under normal physiological conditions.
source: However, STIM-1 knockdown was shown to have no effect on baseline transmission under normal physiological conditions (de Juan-Sanz et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: ER-localized MCTP is a critical regulator of baseline release, short-term plasticity and PHP under physiological conditions.
source: By contrast, our work specifies a role for ER-localized MCTP as a critical regulator of baseline release, short-term plasticity and PHP, under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Loss of MCTP causes increased short-term facilitation, which is generally associated with decreased presynaptic release probability.
source: We further demonstrate that loss of MCTP causes increased short-term facilitation. This effect is generally associated with decreased presynaptic release probability.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with reference to established knowledge about short-term plasticity.

claim: The magnitude of the decrease in baseline release in mctp under physiological calcium conditions is quantitatively similar to that observed in mutations deleting RIM.
source: It is worth noting that the magnitude of the decrease in baseline release in mctp under physiological calcium conditions is quantitatively similar to that observed in mutations deleting Rab3-Interacting Molecule (RIM; Müller et al., 2012), a presynaptic component of the active zone cytomatrix (Südhof, 2012).
evidence: This comparison is made in the Discussion with citations to relevant studies.

claim: PHP can be induced in the absence of action potential induced presynaptic calcium influx.
source: Since PHP can be induced in the absence of action potential induced presynaptic calcium influx (Frank et al., 2006), MCTP would need to be sensitive to changes in extracellular calcium, presumably detecting corresponding changes in cytoplasmic calcium since MCTP resides on the internal ER membranes.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Drosophila S2 cells are mycoplasma negative.
source: Cells are mycoplasma negative (tested by MycoAlert, Lonza, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
